Three of twenty-three · Prepared by Antimony Studio

Same work.
Different argument.

Hot Black's work wins on craft. The published case studies describe the craft and stop. Nothing on the site tells a procurement panel what the work returned to the business that paid for it.

So we took three projects and rebuilt them the way they would read if the Approach page is true. Everything here is built from what Hot Black has already published. The only new material is the argument, and the fields marked in blue, which only Hot Black can fill.

GreyHot Black's own published fact. Nothing added.
InkAntimony's read of the commercial brief, the constraint and the decision.
BlueThe number or the sentence only Hot Black holds. The page is incomplete until these are in.
We factor in the factors: the program, the budget, the motivations and the metrics of success.

Workplace · Banking · Sydney
01

How ANZ moved two thousand people into a building designed to make them choose it.

WhoANZ
WhereSydney CBD, NSW
When2021
How big28,500 sqm · 14 levels
WhyMake a 14-level lease earn attendance in the first year of hybrid.
What it returnedFour fields below. Only ANZ and Hot Black hold the numbers.
Published today

14 levels of urban-city inspired workspace.

Rewritten

Fourteen floors of the same desking is an anonymous building. ANZ needed a place two thousand people would travel to. The answer was a city, with destinations, not a stack of floors.

Photography: Hot Black, as published.
1.1

The brief behind the briefAntimony's read

ANZ set out to redefine the future of working for an almost 2,000-strong Sydney workforce, across 14 levels and 28,500 sqm, completed in 2021.

Strip the language back and the brief is a balance-sheet question. In 2021 a bank committing to 28,500 sqm in the Sydney CBD was betting that people would come back to it. Every floor that stayed empty was a cost with no return. The design had one job before any other: make the lease defensible.

The published version calls this "the future of working." The commercial version is: give two thousand people a reason to travel.

1.2

The constraint

Scale is the enemy of cohesion. Fourteen floors solved identically is cheaper to document and easier to deliver, and it produces a building nobody feels anything about. Layered on top: a reuse target that meant existing furniture had to be absorbed rather than replaced, a sustainability position that had to be material rather than decorative, and an Indigenous acknowledgement that had to be made properly or not at all.

1.3

The decision

A "mini city" concept across the 14 levels. Two anchors outside the working floors: the Client Floor, "the club", built around craftsmanship and detailing for the clientele; and the Venture Lab, warehouse-inspired, deliberately less polished, a space where nothing is ever finished. A custom arrival carpet by Gamilaroi Ularoi/Yuwaalaraay yinarr artist Lakkari Pitt. Pocket parks on Level 14. Existing furniture reused and repurposed wherever possible.

The decision that matters is the one that could have been argued out of the scheme: concentrating the building's identity into two destinations and letting one of them look unfinished. A client floor that signals who pays the bills, and a lab that signals where the business is going. The uniform alternative removes both and saves money in week one. It costs attendance for the length of the lease.

1.4

What it deliveredVerifiable today

Better Future Sydney Design Awards, Gold. Better Future Australia Design Awards, Gold. Better Future WILD Design Awards, Silver. Furniture reuse across the fitout. Indigenous artwork at arrival, not in a corridor. Biophilic relief on L14 for staff to step away from the desk.

Three awards prove the industry rated the craft. They do not prove the lease worked. That proof exists, it sits inside ANZ, and it is the single most persuasive thing Hot Black could put on this page.

1.5

What only Hot Black can addBlue fields

Attendance
Average weekly attendance in the first 12 months, against the pre-move benchmark.
This is the number the brief was written to move.
Reuse
Proportion of existing furniture and fitout retained, and the capital it displaced.

Client floor

Sentiment

The sentence the client would say about what this building did for the business.
Only ANZ can write thisName, title, Property or Workplace function. One sentence about the outcome, not the aesthetic. This single line does more work with a panel than the three awards combined.
Workplace · Technology · Melbourne
02

More people, the same floorplate, and most of the building left standing.

WhoSportsbet
WhereMelbourne CBD, VIC
When2022
How big7,700 sqm
WhyAbsorb the BetEasy merger without a bigger lease or a demolition bill.
What it returnedHeadcount on footprint, and the capital avoided. Fields below.
Published today

An energised, vibrant HQ that doesn't take itself too seriously.

Rewritten

A merger meant more people. The obvious answer was more space. Hot Black's answer was a workplace strategy that fitted them into the building Sportsbet already had, and kept most of it.

Photography: Hot Black, as published.
2.1

The brief behind the briefAntimony's read

Following a merger with BetEasy, Hot Black's role was to re-energise the space and move to a semi-agile neighbourhood methodology that allowed for increased numbers of staff. Retaining as much of the built environment as possible was integral to budget and to minimising waste.

This is the cleanest commercial brief on the Hot Black site and the published page buries it under "home-away-from-home." Two companies became one, headcount went up, and the lease did not. The question was whether design could absorb growth that would otherwise have been solved with property. That is a capital question, and Hot Black answered it.

Every square metre not leased and every wall not demolished is a number. Sportsbet has both.

2.2

The constraint

Hold the budget by keeping the base build. Fit more people into 7,700 sqm while moving to hybrid, which changes desk ratios but only if the strategy is trusted. Connect multiple levels that did not read as one company. And do it for a brand whose obvious fitout is a wall of team colours, which would have dated in a season.

2.3

The decision

Workplace strategy reports first, then a semi-agile neighbourhood model. Environmental graphics and wayfinding as the visual language connecting the levels, drawing on the ball, the field lines and jersey fabric, "thematic but executed with a mature hand." Hub spaces opened to an exposed floorplate for light and views. A previously closed reception brought into the activated podium level. Natural materials and planting throughout.

Two decisions carried the budget. Graphics and wayfinding did the connective work that a rebuild would normally do, at a fraction of the cost. And the strategy was allowed to set the desk ratio, which is the only way more people fit without more floor. The restraint on the sporting theme is the decision a cheaper studio would not have made, and the reason the space still reads well four years on.

2.4

What it deliveredVerifiable today

A merged workforce housed within the existing 7,700 sqm footprint. Built environment substantially retained. Reception opened into the podium floorplan. Light and outlook recovered on the hub levels.

Everything above is on the published page in one form or another. What is missing is the arithmetic. How many more people, how much of the building retained, how much capital the approach avoided. Sportsbet's property and finance teams have those figures to the dollar.

2.5

03

A portfolio of brands, a marketing floor and a working laboratory, consolidated under one roof.

WhoAsahi Beverages
WhereSouthbank, VIC
When2026
How big9,000 sqm
WhyBring a business built by acquisition into one building that behaves like one company.
What it returnedSites consolidated, functions co-located, and what that changed. Fields below.
Published today

Infusing emotion, quality & sensory experience into the workplace.

Rewritten

A beverage group with a family of brands, specialist teams and a fully operational testing lab needed one headquarters that could hold all of it without flattening any of it. The design is a consolidation argument made physical.

Photography: Hot Black, as published.
3.1

The brief behind the briefAntimony's read

Hot Black partnered with Asahi Beverages to redefine their workplace strategy. The workplace brings together a diverse range of specialised functions, from media and marketing teams through to a fully operational beverage testing laboratory, and celebrates Asahi's extensive portfolio and family of brands under one roof.

"Under one roof" is the brief. Asahi in Australia is a business assembled through acquisition, and businesses assembled that way inherit separate buildings, separate cultures and brands that have never shared a floor. A headquarters that only looks good does nothing about that. One that gives each function a place and gives the whole a single narrative is the operational fix.

This is the most recent project on the site. It was published in July 2026 with the same four fields as a project from 2021. The gap is current.

3.2

The constraint

A laboratory inside an office, with the safety and operational performance obligations that carries. Multiple brands with their own equity, which cannot be merged into one visual identity without losing something. Executive and boardroom environments that need permanence next to social zones that need the opposite. And a Melbourne location that the business wanted the building to belong to, rather than a global template dropped into Southbank.

3.3

The decision

A vertical narrative. Each level reveals a different layer of the organisation's story. Social and collaborative zones, "brewed for connection." Executive and boardroom environments, "legacy distilled." Safety, sustainability and operational performance at the core, with the lab fully operational rather than displayed. A locally responsive approach grounded in Melbourne's character.

The decision worth defending is the vertical narrative, because it solves the brand problem without a compromise. No single identity has to win. Each floor carries a layer, and the building reads as one story from the lobby up. The alternative, a neutral corporate shell with brand graphics applied, is what most consolidation headquarters end up with, and it tells staff from the acquired businesses exactly what they expected to hear.

3.4

What it deliveredVerifiable today

9,000 sqm in Southbank, completed 2026. A fully operational beverage testing laboratory within the workplace. Marketing, media and specialist functions co-located. The full brand portfolio represented in one building.

Because this project is three months old, the outcome data is being generated right now. Attendance in the first quarter, the number of previous sites closed, the first survey. Hot Black is in a position no other studio has: the ability to publish the result while the market is still looking at the pictures.

The other twenty

The pattern is the same on every project. Only the numbers change.

Nothing on these three pages needed new design work. The photography, the project facts and the design thinking were all already published. What was missing was an argument, and four or five numbers that live inside the client.

That is the gap between a studio that competes on craft and a studio that competes on craft and evidence. Every practice in the field that does both is multi-city or global. No studio at Hot Black's scale does. Hot Black has the client list to be the first, and the material is already in the archive.

Twelve of the twenty-three are workplace. The same five-row structure, the same four blue fields and the same quote slot apply to every one. The property-facing projects (181 William, 177 Pacific Highway, Gateway) need a leasing-velocity version of the fields. The hospitality projects (Ette, Huff, Brunetti, Bang Bang) need a trading version. The structure holds. The fields change.
